entry.title: India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investmentIndia can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investment

Emerging-market investment is grounded in this promise. Indian asset prices have an imperfect correlation with the global portfolio and hence offer gains from diversification

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty

Ajay Shah6 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:36 PM ISTEvery finance expert knows the power of diversification. We diversify across firms in an industry. We diversify across industries in a country. We diversify across countries. At each stage, we get a risk reduction. Harry Markowitz famously observed that diversification is the only free lunch observed in all economics. When a portfolio holds assets with uncorrelated returns, risk is quenched, and human welfare is enhanced.  This foundational logic provides the original basis for internationalised asset management. Cross-border capital flows create conditions in which all participants become better off through diversification and risk sharing. The desired state is where an Indian family owns a flat in Tokyo and rents it out to a resident while a Japanese family owns a flat in Bombay and rents it out to a resident. Each owner insulates the balance sheet from the home country risk. If India fares badly, the Tokyo asset continues to work well for the Indian owner, and vice versa. Each owner is well protected as compared to owning a flat in her or his own city. The pursuit of this protection, of this reduction of financial portfolio risk, drives capital across borders.  Emerging-market investment is grounded in this promise. Indian asset prices have an imperfect correlation with the global portfolio and hence offer gains from diversification. But their prices have to be driven down by market forces to compensate for the high risk of investing in India. Indian capital controls, taxation, policy risk, and the threat of expropriation by the state: All these drive up the required rate of return for a global investor to buy Indian assets (ie they drive down Indian asset prices). These policy choices act as a tax on capital, raising its cost. The central benefit for foreigners investing in India is the structural gain from diversification. The macroeconomic and political shocks in India are different from the shocks seen elsewhere, so investing in India is attractive.  Some unusual things happened in the past decade, and those complicated this pretty picture. There was a sustained big divergence, where the United States (US) economy did well and the Indian economy didn’t. The relevant metric for a global allocator is the dollar return, where depreciation in the exchange rate acts as a haircut on local equity gains. If we superpose the S&P 500 against the Indian Nifty 50, expressed in dollars, over the last nine years, we see that the Nifty grew from 100 to about 170. But the S&P 500 grew from 100 to 275. This is a large gap in performance: 6.44 per cent vs 11.48 per cent in dollars, on average. In these nine years, the gains from diversification into India went with a significant drag in average returns.  Nothing has changed in the finance theory! Diversification remains a free lunch. Financial markets process information efficiently. All information is contained in the price, so past performance is not relevant for future performance. The 95 per cent confidence interval for the annual S&P 500 return, based on this data, runs from —1.09 per cent to 25.65 per cent and for the Nifty it is — 5.42 per cent to 19.78 per cent: Hardly a strong foundation to make claims about the future. But such a performance gap over a nine-year period weighs on many practical people. The curious combination of superior US stock-market performance with sluggish Indian stock-market performance, over a nine-year period, has had a force of its own.  While financial markets are quite efficient, decision making in financial intermediation is often less than rational. Asset allocators operate in institutional settings defined by investment committees and career risk. The theoretical mandate to diversify, to not care about past performance, clashes with the institutional pressure to chase the assets that recently outperformed.  This unique backdrop has generated a drag against foreign investment into India. When the dominant global asset class delivers exceptional returns, the appetite to underwrite the institutional frictions of emerging markets diminishes. The bar for the entry of foreign capital rises, and the flow of global savings into Indian assets faces a structural headwind.  We should not overstate the macroeconomic problem caused by this dynamic. Sanjuktha Athreya demonstrated that it was a stall, not a reversal (https://bit.ly/IndiaStall). Capital did not flee, but it stopped arriving at the previous rate. The macroeconomic impact of this stall was muted by domestic conditions. There was poor corporate investment in India in this period. The macroeconomic identity links the current-account deficit to the gap between domestic investment and domestic savings. Because corporate capital expenditure was weak, the demand for capital was low, so the gap between investment and savings in India was weak. Consequently, there was no great need for inflows of foreign capital. The economy did not face a financing constraint that foreign savings had to resolve, so softness in capital inflows was not a problem.  If artificial intelligence and tech fever in US asset pricing cools, this could potentially induce global investors think about international portfolio formation in a more normal way. A moderation in US equity returns would assist allocators in returning to more orthodox, more theoretically sound strategies. It would restore the traditional focus on international diversification and the pursuit of uncorrelated returns across global markets. This would be good for India.  If foreign investors took more interest in India — and if the Indian authorities removed policy mistakes that impede inflows of foreign capital — then there would be a greater interest in Indian assets. This would exert a causal impact on Indian economic growth through the following path. First, Indian asset prices would go up. For example, when foreigners take an interest in India (and the Indian authorities do not come in the way), Indian corporate bond yields go down. Second, firms would find more investment projects attractive when asset prices are higher. A firm with a high price-earning ratio does more investment than a firm with a low one; a firm with a cheap cost of debt does more investment than a firm with high cost of debt. Such a surge of investment would help growth in gross domestic product. Equal treatment for foreigners by the Indian state remains a powerful lever to push Indian economic growth, and it’s not that hard to do.

entry.title: India's food processing growth needs better storage and farm market reforms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's food processing growth needs better storage and farm market reformsIndia's food processing growth needs better storage and farm market reforms

Apart from permitting 100% FDI through the automatic route, the government has extended the benefits of the production-linked incentive scheme to this industry

premium

Representative Picture

Surinder Sud4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:46 PM ISTThat the country’s food-processing industry has grown rapidly over the past few years is fairly evident. But whether this growth is good enough for a sector that is so vital for agricultural development and has received abundant support and handholding from the government is a moot point.  The sector’s annual growth in the recent past consistently exceeded 7 per cent. This is markedly higher than the manufacturing sector’s growth of around 6 per cent. Yet, only a fraction of the output of cereals, fruit, vegetables, milk, spices, and other farm products is subjected to industrial-scale processing. The bulk of the post-production management of food, including preliminary- and secondary-level processing, takes place in the unorganised sector. Traditional methods of food preservation, such as salting, solar dehydration, fermentation, and pickling (making achaars and murabbas) continue to dominate. Food wastage is rampant at every stage of the post-harvest value chain.  The present worth of the food-processing industry is reckoned at around $382 billion. A recent report, prepared jointly by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci) and Deloitte, a consultancy agency, expects it to swell to over $600 billion by 2030. The expansion is projected to be driven primarily by branded, processed, and premium food products, rather than by higher farm output alone.  However, the food-processing industry handles only 12-14 per cent of food output. This compares poorly with the average processing level of about 35 per cent in some other developing countries, and 48 per cent in developed ones. What is worse, India is unlikely to catch up with the global trend even in the near future, given the government’s none too ambitious goal of raising the food-processing level to 25 per cent by 2030. This target, obviously, requires a revisit, considering the pressing need for some kind of a preservative treatment for food to achieve multiple objectives, such as reducing wastage, facilitating year-round availability of the seasonal produce, and enhancing the value and consumer appeal of the food products. At present, the loss of food during pre-harvest, harvesting, and post-harvest handling is, in some cases, as high as 40-50 per cent. The cost of these losses is estimated at ₹1.55 trillion-2 trillion annually.  Fortunately, the government’s policy framework for food processing seems conducive to fast-tracking the development of this sector. Apart from permitting 100 per cent foreign direct investment (FDI) through the automatic route, the government has extended the benefits of the production-linked incentive scheme to this industry. As a result, this sector has received a cumulative FDI of $16.15 billion since 2000. However, much more investment, foreign and domestic, is called for to boost the utilisation of the untapped food-processing potential.  India is among the world’s leading producers of perishable and semi-perishable farm products, which are numerous and whose quality begins to deteriorate soon after harvest for want of suitable protective treatment. Fruit & vegetables, of which India is the world’s second-largest producer, can be a case in point. Less than 2 per cent of horticultural output, estimated at 387 million tonnes in 2025-26, undergoes post-harvest treatment for waste mitigation, shelf-life prolongation, and utility upgrade. This is woefully inadequate. In the case of milk, where India is the world’s largest producer, hardly round 20 per cent of output is processed into value-enriched products. The rest is marketed as raw milk through unorganised routes.  Fishery is another sector where the scale of processing is too meagre vis-à-vis the size of the catch from the seas and natural water bodies, and the rapidly surging production from aquaculture farms. Given the fast-decaying nature of the fishery products, immediate preservative measures are essential to avert large-scale spoilage.  Spices are another category of products where the level of processing and value augmentation is rather scanty. Though India is the world’s largest grower of these condiments, the bulk of them are marketed, and even exported, without any processing, barring cleaning, grinding and packaging. Only a tiny part of the production is used to produce high-value items like oleoresins, extracts, and essential oils.  That said, the fact also is that the food-processing sector is beset with several formidable challenges that are impeding its smooth growth. The most daunting among them are states’ restrictive laws on marketing agricultural produce, which bind processing companies to procure their raw material from regular mandis, instead of purchasing it directly from the producers. The others include the bar on contract farming, which could facilitate the regular supply of processable foodstuff, and the paucity of refrigerated transportation and cold-storage capacity. These snags need to be addressed to woo greater investment in food-processing units, especially those churning out convenient and ready-to-consume food products.

entry.title: Ask businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunities
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Ask businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunitiesAsk businesses why they pass up export and investment opportunities

The government has been amending the guidelines and constituting committees to oversee implementation of the schemes

premium

Representative Picture

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 11:10 PM ISTIn February this year, the government unveiled several subsidy schemes under its Export Promotion Mission (EPM). Under some schemes, it appears, not enough exporters are coming forward to claim the subsidies. Last week, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade issued some trade notices relaxing the eligibility criteria, increasing airfare reimbursement rates and so on.  The EPM operates through two integrated sub-schemes, ‘Niryat Protsahan’, which facilitates access to trade finance, and ‘Niryat Disha’, which supports market access and addresses non-financial barriers to exports.  The six Niryat Disha interventions  are Market Access Support (MAS) to help organize/participate in trade fairs, exhibitions, buyer-seller meets and trade delegations, including airfare reimbursement for eligible participants; Trade Regulations, Accreditation and Compliance Enablement (TRACE) for partial reimbursement of eligible testing, inspection and certification costs to meet overseas requirements; Logistics Interventions for Freight and Transport (LIFT) for partial freight reimbursement for eligible micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in identified low export-intensity districts; Integrated Support for Trade Intelligence and Facilitation (INSIGHT) for supporting market intelligence, information on trade requirements and guidance to help firms identify and pursue export opportunities; Facilitating Logistics, Overseas Warehousing and Fulfilment (FLOW) for supporting access to overseas warehousing and order fulfilment infrastructure, including support for ecommerce exports; and the scheme for global outreach for branding, labelling and export packaging to help expand and sustain global markets for Indian goods and services by developing a unified brand India framework.  The government has been amending the guidelines and constituting committees to oversee implementation of the schemes.  Last Tuesday, the government enhanced the maximum eligible export turnover for availing airfare reimbursement under the MAS from ₹75 lakh in the preceding year to ₹50 crore, raised the airfare reimbursement limit up to 95 per cent for MSMEs and 80 per cent for other eligible entities, within monetary ceilings and reduced the mandatory membership period with export promotion councils from six to three months. Under the TRACE scheme, the government increased the number of testing, inspection, and certification entries eligible for reimbursement from 462 to 600.  Under the LIFT scheme, the government expanded the coverage of low export-intensity districts to 308 listed districts, expanded the categories of eligible gateways to include Land Customs Stations and Integrated Check Posts with an attached Container Freight Station, added inland waterways to the existing modes of transport, extended the air freight support for export shipments to Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, in addition to the North Eastern Region, reduced the minimum qualifying inland haul from 200 kilometre (km) to 100 km, with reimbursement limited to 400 km and extended the support to all exportable merchandise items, except those specified in the negative list of export products/categories.  It is too early to say how exporters will respond to these amendments, but one point is getting clear. The exporters will take the subsidies on offer if the activity itself, say air travel or participating in an exhibition, is justified on commercial considerations. A subsidy may tip the balance sometimes. Similarly, businesses may welcome the subsidies under the Production Linked Incentive and other schemes, income tax rate cuts, GST rate cuts, improved market access through trade agreements and so on but will invest only when it makes commercial sense.  The government should ask businesses which obstacles most often cause them to let go export or investment opportunities.

entry.title: The decade India turned the tide on poverty
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The decade India turned the tide on povertyThe decade India turned the tide on poverty

The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back

Union Minister for Finance & Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman | Image: Bloomberg

Nirmala Sitharaman6 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTA year ago, during my visit to Kiphire, an aspirational district in the remote hills of Nagaland, I interacted with tribal women from local self-help groups. Among them was Esther, a Lakhpati Didi, who proudly spoke of her millet-based products reaching customers online, far beyond Nagaland. What stayed with me was their confidence in a better future. I encouraged them to dream bigger and become Crorepati Didis. Their stories reflected a transformation reaching India's remotest corners, where geographical and economic challenges have long constrained opportunities, yet aspirations for a better tomorrow are growing. When the World Bank released its Poverty & Equity Brief on India last month, my interaction in Kiphire came back to me. The report showed that nearly 50 crore Indians had moved out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, while extreme poverty has been almost eradicated. These figures captured the transformation I had witnessed firsthand.  It was not always so. For over six decades after Independence, eradicating mass poverty remained an unfulfilled promise. Even in the early 2010s, India was portrayed abroad as a home of enduring destitution, lagging in sanitation, nutrition, clean cooking fuel and banking. The prevailing prescription was simply to put money into the hands of the poor, and poverty would take care of itself. The last decade has overturned that belief. Under PM Narendra Modi’s leadership, India has witnessed a fundamental shift from temporary relief to removing the barriers that perpetuate poverty. Guided by Antyodaya, the welfare of the last person in the line, our Government chose the harder path of addressing deprivations, household by household, ensuring development reached those who needed it most. Targeted, focused and tailored

 Garibi is not merely a shortage of income or wages. A household without a secure roof, safe water, sanitation or healthcare remains vulnerable even when its income rises. One illness can wipe out savings and push a family back into poverty. Our government, therefore, made every intervention targeted at those who needed it, focused on measurable outcomes and tailored to the deprivation it was meant to remove. There was no magic wand. Each scheme required careful identification of beneficiaries, effective delivery and follow-up until the last household was reached. PM Modi has personally and painstakingly monitored implementation, intervened at critical junctures to resolve bottlenecks, ensured follow-ups and encouraged the use of technology to track delivery. This sustained attention has helped translate policy into tangible improvements in people’s lives. Health and dignity begin at home A family cannot climb out of poverty while illness and the daily burden of fetching water keep pulling it back. Under Swachh Bharat, access to household toilets has improved sanitation and helped avert an estimated 60,000-70,000 infant deaths a year. Jal Jeevan Mission has expanded rural tap-water connections from about 3 crore households in 2019 to nearly 16 crore, sparing women and girls the long walk for water and reducing exposure to waterborne diseases. Ujjwala Yojana has enabled cleaner, smokeless kitchens, while PM Awas Yojana has provided the security and dignity of pucca homes. Ayushman Bharat, offering cashless hospital care, has strengthened financial protection against medical expenses. Together, they act as insurance against the shocks that once pushed families back into poverty, while lowering household expenditure and freeing time for work. From a bank account to an enterprise Protection keeps families from slipping back into poverty; to rise further, they need opportunities to earn. For crores of people, that journey began with a bank account. Once, it was accepted that only fifteen paise of every rupee sent from the exchequer reached the intended citizen. Direct Benefit Transfer has changed that. Over 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts enable benefits to reach recipients directly, without middlemen. Technology has made this possible at an unprecedented scale. A bank account also provides a safe place for savings and helps establish a financial record, opening doors to formal credit. For those without property, access to the first loan can be life-changing. Two months ago, during an interaction with MUDRA beneficiaries, I met Sushmita Gharai from West Bengal. She lost her father during the pandemic, and her family’s printing business subsequently collapsed. With no land or gold as security, a collateral-free MUDRA loan helped her restart the press. Today, she employs 8 people, twice her initial workforce, and plans to expand into digital printing. What stayed with me was her determination to rebuild and grow. Her story reflects the aspirations of countless young Indians whose ambition exceeds their financial means. Under MUDRA, 60 crore loan accounts have been sanctioned, about two-thirds to women, while PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma support street vendors and traditional artisans. Women have led this transformation. Ten crore rural women participate in SHGs that, through the DAY-NRLM and other programmes, have become platforms for savings, skills, credit and entrepreneurship. Over 3.7 crore women have become Lakhpati Didis, with some going further to become Crorepati Didis. Others, trained as Namo Drone Didis, now provide drone-spraying services to farmers. Women once excluded from economic opportunity are building enterprises and livelihoods of their own. The Sankalp for Viksit Bharat For generations, poverty was treated as something India could manage but never end. What appeared unimaginable a decade ago has now been achieved through years of steady work on the ground. Yet this is no time to rest; the road to Viksit Bharat by 2047 brings its own challenges. The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back. The protection offered via various measures must now be complemented by even wider access to finance, markets and the digital economy. Government is building closer links between academia and industry through employment-linked incentives, internships and apprenticeships, while investment in infrastructure is connecting the country as never before. Opportunity cannot remain the preserve of a few.  The Prime Minister has said that Viksit Bharat, like freedom, is a commitment that every Indian must live. Having achieved in ten years what remained unfulfilled for six decades, India can face the next twenty with confidence. With the resolve of 140 crore Indians, Viksit Bharat by 2047 is within our reach, and we together will get there.

entry.title: Tax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatmentTax exemption for housing, but why not for MFs? A case for equal treatment

Tax exemptions favour NRIs and housing investments over resident investors in financial assets

premium

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:29 PM ISTDharam, a non-resident Indian (NRI), was discussing the revamping of his equity portfolio with me. He had been an NRI for decades and built up a substantial share portfolio by remitting money from overseas. He now wanted to sell and consolidate into an equity index fund. But the tax law put him in a piquant situation. If he sold his shares and bought other shares, the entire capital gain would be exempt under Section 115F of the Income Tax Act, 1961. But an equity mutual fund would attract full capital gains tax. “If attracting and retaining foreign currency into Indian equity shares was the motivation behind providing this exemption, then why are equity mutual funds not covered under this section?” he wondered. The law seemed to favour concentrated equity exposure and taxes diversification.  I remembered this conversation as I read that the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) had recommended concessions on long-term capital gains tax to the finance ministry. Sebi has reportedly asked for the long-term capital gains tax on foreign portfolio investors to be scrapped. It has also reportedly recommended that a switch from one mutual fund scheme to another should not be treated as a sale. A possible reading is that no tax would be charged when money moves from one equity mutual fund scheme to another after a year. This is like a gift or an inheritance. The receiver pays no tax on receipt. The giver’s cost and purchase date pass on to the receiver, who pays tax only on the final sale. The tax is postponed, not removed. The foreign investor may get an exemption. The resident investor may get only a postponement.  Back to Dharam’s question. I explained that the exemption was not discrimination against mutual funds. It was inserted in 1983 to help with the balance of payments situation. It allowed reinvestment in shares, debentures, deposits and government securities but not mutual funds. At that time, Unit Trust of India was the only mutu-al fund, and the industry was in its infancy.  Section 54EA, inserted in 1996, was a wider tax exemption. It covered all taxpayers and all long-term capital gains, if the sale consideration was invested in equity initial public offerings (IPOs) or mutual funds. The exemption was discontinued in 2000. One reason cited was that the low long-term capital gains tax rate left little justification for the exemption. Ironically, the same Budget widened the exemption for reinvesting capital gains in residential property. A taxpayer who already owned one house could now buy another and still claim it. The low-rate argument applied to all long-term gains. It was not applied to housing.  Twenty-four years later, the Union Budget of July 2024 broadly harmonised long-term capital gains tax rates, and the finance minister said every asset class has to be treated similarly. But neutrality needs more than uniform rates. It must extend to exemptions. Today the regime treats residents and mutual funds less favourably than NRIs and housing.  There are good reasons to encourage investment in housing and to attract foreign money into Indian markets. There are equally good reasons to encourage investment by residents in financial assets. How can the law exempt an entrepreneur who sells shares in his business to buy a second home, yet tax a retiree who sells equity shares to build a mutual fund portfolio for retirement income?  Truth be told, Dharam was luckier than that retiree. He found a workaround. He got the exemption and still diversified by investing in a portfolio of shares advised by a portfolio manager. Resident investors do not have even this tax advantage. Yet they are taken for granted, perhaps because they have nowhere else to go. Postponing tax on mutual fund switches is just a start. It is not enough. Residents reinvesting long-term capital gains in mutual funds or equity shares should get an exemption along the lines of the erstwhile Section 54EA with the same lock-in and cap that housing carries. After 26 years, it is time to reverse the decision made in 2000.

entry.title: Beyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningful
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Beyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningfulBeyond the Jan Dhan passbook: Making financial inclusion more meaningful

Banks deepen financial inclusion when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding

premium

ILLUSTRATION: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Tamal Bandyopadhyay8 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 10:00 PM ISTIn January 2025, South Andaman's official newsletter recorded a visit by senior administrators to a Jarawa settlement at Jirkatang to hand over voter identity cards to 19 members of the tribe, marking the Jarawa's first inclusion in the electoral roll. It was an electoral exercise, not a banking camp. Yet, it carries a lesson for every public institution: Service must move towards people, not wait for people to find it.  Another archival record, a presentation hosted by the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, notes that insurance premiums were paid for 32 Onge individuals under the Janashree Bima Yojana from 2007, alongside livelihood support through the Onge Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society.  Such episodes capture what financial inclusion ought to mean: Recognition, access and protection tailored to how people actually live.  The finance ministry's Nationwide Financial Inclusion Saturation Campaign, running from 21 October to 31 December, gives India's banking system another chance to put that principle into practice. Steered by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), the drive covers 270,000 gram panchayats and urban local bodies across the country.  Going beyond account opening, camps run by banks, led by public sector lenders, are tackling a set of operational bottlenecks: Re-KYC (know your customer) for Jan Dhan and regular savings accounts, pending Central KYC identifiers, nomination updates for accounts and lockers, revival of inoperative accounts, and enrolment under the micro-insurance and pension schemes.  Former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Y V Reddy coined the phrase "financial inclusion" while drafting the annual policy statement for 2006-07, released in April 2006, with Deputy Governor Usha Thorat. The term may have arrived in 2006, but Indian banking's push into the hinterland began in the late 1960s, with bank nationalisation and directed credit to neglected sectors and weaker sections. In the 1970s, the RBI laid down priority sector lending norms; experiments followed with regional rural banks, the self-help group–bank linkage programme and local area banks.  The current campaign is different in design. It is about fixing the plumbing of existing accounts.  In West Bengal, the State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC) is working with member banks, district administrations, panchayats and municipalities, with a sharp focus on households from Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups.  In Punjab, SLBC convenor Punjab National Bank, peer lenders and district collectors are prioritising the revival of inoperative accounts across 13,236 village panchayats and 166 urban local bodies, backed by 7,669 bank branches and 98 financial literacy centres.  RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Saturday inaugurated a special financial inclusion camp at Vaksai in Maharashtra,  organised by Bank of Maharashtra. It focuses on re-KYC of bank accounts and expanding access to banking services.   Meanwhile, State Bank of India, which is the SLBC convenor in Assam and its neighbouring states, is steering the drive across Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura.  At the North-East Bankers' Conclave 3.0, held in Aizawl in October, the government reported that banks had opened 131 branches and installed 126 ATMs in the region between December 2024 and March 2026, and that 6,905 of 9,479 identified villages were now connected to either a bank branch or an India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) outlet. This progress predates the current drive. Of the remaining 2,574 villages, 2,515 will be linked through IPPB and 59 through brick-and-mortar branches.  The next phase of that expansion rests on a crucial regulatory tweak, announced at the same conclave. Elsewhere in India, the guideline for opening a brick-and-mortar branch requires a minimum population of 3,000. In the North-East, where difficult terrain and scattered hamlets make single-village thresholds unworkable, that norm has been lowered to 2,000 and applied on a cluster basis, allowing banks to pool adjacent villages to justify a central branch.  Yet bricks-and-mortar alone is not enough. Physical reach must be matched by explanations in the local language and reliable follow-up. The best camp is one where visitors walk away understanding both the service they received and their next step.  For communities such as the Jarawa and the Onge of the Andaman Islands, inclusion must also respect distinct social identities. Policy towards the Jarawa rightly emphasises protection from intrusive outside contact and the preservation of their social structure, subsistence and culture. In September 2025, the islands' cooperative newsletter noted that the Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank has 41 branches across 14 islands, while highlighting the role of Ellon Hinengo Ltd and the Tribal Development Cooperative Society in fostering tribal economic self-reliance.  On the ground, practical questions decide whether inclusion sticks. Who explains the form, corrects a clerical error and stays reachable after the camp packs up? Banks deepen inclusion only when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding, never through target-driven enrolment pressure.  Launched on 28 August 2014, the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) remains the bedrock passbook of this effort. As of 4 November 2026, PMJDY had 597 million beneficiaries, 333 million of them women and 463.4 million banked at rural and semi-urban branches. Together they hold Rs3.28 trillion in deposits and 419 million RuPay cards. Public sector banks carry the bulk of the load with 459 million accounts, while regional rural banks hold another 112 million.  Now consider how the camp priorities are trying to make those accounts work harder.  To ease re-KYC friction, the RBI in June 2025 allowed banks to use authorised business correspondents to collect self-declarations from customers whose KYC details are unchanged or where only the address has changed, subject to safeguards, while keeping the bank accountable for completing the update.  For dormant money, the RBI's UDGAM (Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation) portal lets citizens search for unclaimed balances across banks in one place. Deposits left unclaimed for 10 years move to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, yet depositors or their legal heirs can claim them at any time, with no time limit.  Social security forms the next pillar. The Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) offers life cover of Rs 2 lakh for death from any cause at an annual premium of Rs 436. Open to account holders aged 18 to 50 and renewable up to the age of 55, it is a pure term cover with no maturity value, and new or rejoining subscribers face a 30-day waiting period for deaths other than by accident. By 22 July 2026, cumulative enrolments stood at 280.6 million with over 1 million claims settled up to 30 June 2026.  Along with it, the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) gives account holders aged 18 to 70 a cover of Rs 2 lakh for accidental death or permanent total disability (and Rs 1 lakh for permanent partial disability) for Rs 20 a year. Cumulative enrolments reached 591 million by 22 July 2026, with 189,057 claims disbursed up to 30 June 2026. Crucially, PMSBY is an accident cover, not a health policy; it does not reimburse hospital bills.  Both schemes rely on consent-based auto-debit and annual renewal. Consent matters because a family that knows a policy exists is far more likely to file a timely claim. Rather than touting cumulative enrolments alone, banks and insurers should publish the number of active policies, renewal success rates and lapses. Debiting a premium from a Jan Dhan account does not automatically translate into effective protection.  Can a bereaved family identify the insurer, recognise the premium debit in a passbook and navigate the claim paperwork? Banks' duty of care must extend to renewal alerts, minimum-balance reminders, help with documentation and claim channels that people can understand.  Similarly, the Atal Pension Yojana (APY) guarantees a minimum monthly pension of between Rs 1,000 and Rs 5,000 after the age of 60 to citizens who join between the ages of 18 and 40, do not pay income tax and contribute regularly until retirement. As of 8 November 2026, APY had 81 million active subscribers and Rs 60,299 crore in assets under management. Because APY is a long-term contributory commitment, not a free dole, bankers must explain contribution obligations and exit rules clearly before signing anyone up.  The Jarawa electoral roll was an act of civic recognition, not an insurance drive. But its lesson for banking is unmistakable: Institutions earn trust when they listen, return and see the job through, turning financial inclusion from a form-filling exercise into an enduring relationship.  _____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. entry.title: 'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereignty
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / 'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereignty'Kill switch': A new front in the global chip wars over tech sovereignty

Remote feature inside semiconductor chips threatens national sovereignty, raising fresh alarms across global tech industry

premium

The growing use of telemetry and remote-control features in semiconductors is raising concerns over potential hardware kill switches, with implications for national security and technological sovereignty.

Pranjal Sharma4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:44 PM ISTSemiconductor chips are becoming as critical to our survival as electricity. From home appliances to industrial machines to mobility, the semiconductor is the heart pumping intelligence into industry’s veins.  The war over chips has exploded with the Nvidia crisis. Even as the story captures global attention, the question of manufacturing, selling and controlling chips has become a top priority for governments.  The US and China are locked in a complex struggle to maintain their autonomy despite their interdependence in chip manufacturing and usage. Both countries want to control not only the export of chips, but also how they are used — via telemetry.  As chipmakers can remotely shut down semiconductors through these tracking systems, the prospect of a hardware “kill switch” has created a new risk for national technological sovereignty.  Telemetry in semiconductor chips refers to the built-in capability of a chip to measure, monitor and report its own operating conditions and performance in real time. It has become a critical feature in modern processors, artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators, networking chips and automotive semiconductors. Chips are so complex that they cannot be managed efficiently without continuous visibility into their behaviour.  By providing continuous operational insights, telemetry helps optimise performance, improve energy efficiency, prevent overheating, enhance reliability and predict potential failures.  Telemetry has a superpower, too: It can be used to kill a semiconductor remotely. It can shut down a chip automatically or trigger a controlled shutdown of the host system when certain conditions are detected.  Telemetry alone does not shut down a chip. Instead, it provides the data that a security policy, management controller or firmware function uses to decide whether a shutdown or restriction should occur. For example, if on-chip sensors detect that temperatures have exceeded a safe operating limit, the chip can initiate an emergency shutdown to prevent permanent damage.  Semiconductor chips can be designed to be remotely shut down, disabled or restricted in functionality. This capability depends entirely on the chip’s architecture, firmware, security features, and the system in which it is deployed. While the semiconductor manufacturer designs these shutdown mechanisms, the buyer also has a say through licensing and purchase agreements.  In the semiconductor industry, remote disabling is typically implemented through software, firmware or licensing controls rather than by physically cutting power to the silicon. If a chip detects a violation of licensing, security, export-control or usage policies, it may refuse to boot, block specific workloads, disable accelerators or lock itself into a restricted operating mode.  Chips sold in general commercial markets and operating independently usually do not have a kill switch. Manufacturers do not share much about this publicly. The switch is not an inherent capability of all semiconductor chips. It must be deliberately built into the chip’s hardware and software.  So far, there has been no widely documented case in which a company such as Nvidia, AMD or Intel has publicly acknowledged remotely disabling deployed commercial chips due to an export-control violation. Yet as the war over AI hots up, the next batch of chips shipped to global markets may well have a kill switch baked into them — and customers may not even realise it exists.  The prospect of a kill switch is raising severe concerns across industry and government. Triggering a remote shutdown can directly undermine a country's technological sovereignty. For instance, semiconductors powering an active defence system could be switched off remotely if the chip manufacturer is obliged to do so under export-control conditions.  Kill switches can be weaponised across critical sectors such as enterprise servers and Cloud infrastructure, telecommunications equipment, industrial control systems and connected vehicles. The justification for using a kill switch may vary but the impact will be the same: A foreign-made semiconductor could pose a serious risk.  The writer is an economic analyst and author   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openlyIndia Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly

One big cause of Mr Modi's frustration is corporate India's unwillingness to pass on the benefits of tax cuts to employees through raises, hiring, or investment

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the inaugural session of FICCI’s Annual General Meeting and Annual Convention. | Image credit: FICCI (X)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 10:12 AM ISTThe most apt description for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s mass admonition of corporate India at the Ficci annual general meeting is that it was a cri de coeur. I use this even as I’m reminded of the late and venerable D N Singh, my first news editor at The Indian Express in 1977. He had banned “foreign” words in our writing. English is foreign enough for all of us, he’d say. In this case, however, a cry from the heart doesn’t fully capture where the Prime Minister was coming from. The dictionary tells us that a cri de coeur is more profound. It’s a “passionate, heartfelt appeal, protest, even an outcry”. The Prime Minister spoke in anger, frustration, helplessness even. What more can I do to get you guys moving? It was way more fraught than a mere cry from the heart.  It’s a bit like a general failing to implore his troops to assault a hill despite a thousand war cries, words of inspiration, even a dash of “spirit”. Since we started with a bit of French, that “spirit” reference is from the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo. While his original line, as recorded in history, was less dramatic, Christopher Plummer, playing Wellington in the 1970 film Waterloo, tells the Duchess of Richmond, who wants to know where his troops get their inspiration to fight: “Gin is the spirit of their patriotism.” I’m avoiding the full quote because the Prime Minister certainly didn’t want to call corporate India ‘scum, beggars and scoundrels,’ as Wellington called his troops. It’s just that his frustration is as profound.

Also Read

Doing our bit: India Inc responds to PM's wake-up call on jobs and pay

PM 'rattled', realised he will be 'outgoing PM' soon, says Congress

Nepal PM's 2-day India visit: Rail link, trading post on the cards

Technology created vistas for cultural connectivity, says PM Modi

Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?premium

 What’s the spirit that a government can offer entrepreneurship? It can be many things: Deregulation, minimum government, fair market supervision, fiscal discipline, freedom from licensing and investment restrictions. And certainly, the gin equivalent of this “spiritual” package would be tax cuts. One big cause of Mr Modi’s frustration is corporate India’s unwillingness to pass this benefit on to employees through raises, hiring or investment. This hasn’t happened even as corporate profits have risen. These troops are unwilling, either too scared to assault that hill or simply too comfortable in safety, pocketing the tax breaks. Let’s read some of Mr Modi’s words to Ficci. “In 2014, the basic corporate tax rate was 30 per cent. We reduced it to 22 per cent. Today, there’s no income tax on earnings up to ~12 lakh in India.” And then he turns the knife. “I know you won’t clap, because however much one gives, your appetite never seems to be satisfied. (aap ka pet nahin bharta). Did you increase the salaries of your employees? Did you increase the number of employees? No. The attitude remains: ‘Modi ji, you do it, we will see’.” While India Inc was left licking its wounded pride, the Congress quickly latched on to the Prime Minister’s words. Isn’t this what we’ve been saying all along, it hit back. Jairam Ramesh was first out of the blocks. “For the first time in 12 years, a nervous and rattled PM has pulled up the captains of industry... (who) must have been taken aback and shocked.” In an elaborate post on X, he blamed not businesses but the government for this stall. He blamed it on crony capitalism, regulatory capture, “an atmosphere of fear and intimidation”, and the unleashing of “investigative agencies”. He concluded by suggesting the Prime Minister look inwards. Rahul Gandhi, on his speaking tour in the United States, also said: We told you so. It’s not my place here to hold forth on the state of the economy. But we know corporate India hasn’t been investing, expanding and hiring, at least nowhere near what 7 per cent-plus growth would indicate. Startups are rising, but largely there’s an entrepreneurship freeze. Much of the growth comes from government spending, especially in heavy infrastructure. If corporate India looks so risk-averse, this isn’t a sudden development. The mood has been festering for years. Some complain of a lack of demand, others say regulation is asphyxiating. Still too many forms need to be filled for too many small things, even something as virtuous as exports. Because, I suppose, the Reserve Bank of India wants to track every dollar that comes in. And, of course, everything in triplicate please. The government may have loosened policies here and there, but the bureaucratic grip is tighter than before. A quick quiz, and no Googling. Can you name the ministers of mines, pharmaceuticals and steel? I mention these three because the Prime Minister highlighted corporate India’s failures specifically in these areas. Why do we export raw materials like iron ore, have so much bauxite, yet import finished steel and specialised aluminium alloys? How come, despite robust pharma exports, we remain dependent on China for APIs, or active pharmaceutical ingredients? With key ministers too lightweight or distracted by party work, and power centralised in the PMO, which is obviously far too overburdened to attend to everything, discretion devolves to the bureaucracies. Corporate India is resigned to this. It’s buying peace in the manner it knows best: Distributing some of the spoils in a way that’s entirely legal and above board, but also revealing. Check out the number of retiring secretaries, especially in the finance ministry, finding sinecures on the boards of influential companies and as chairpersons of almost all significant private-sector banks, and the recently listed stock market titan, NSE (National Stock Exchange). The more the Modi government thinks it’s reforming — and reforming it is — the more it does so in a way that passes power into the hands of the bureaucracy. Corporate India buys peace with them in advance, merely by dropping hints. Here’s the paradox. This is a super-strong government with a very weak implementation spine. As a result, what’s decentralised at the top gathers in the middle. A strong government isn’t immune to policy confusion. On the contrary, it can be prone to flip-flop-flips given its overwhelming power. Long term capital gains (LTCG) tax is a big discussion point now. Count how many changes this government has brought in. The same goes for taxes on dividends. Since 1991, successive finance ministers have said that the essence of a reformed economy lies in moderate, predictable taxes. You most certainly cannot say the same about this government, which also taxes individuals at almost twice the rate of corporations. It’s also been breathtaking in its use of sovereign power. A striking example is the retrospective changes it made to sovereign gold bonds to suit itself and cover for those brilliant people who floated these without hedging for gold prices. The message is an old one. In India, the government, the almighty Sarkar-e-Hind, can never be wrong. Corporate India has a lot to answer for, but for some, the chappal is on the government’s foot. On copper and aluminium imports, two of the largest projects have been shut under activist pressure. If this government has failed to move on these, it cannot blame India Inc. Sadly, corporate India knows this, but nobody would dare speak up. They whisper dark things on the sidelines. But in front of an angry Prime Minister, or the finance minister who’s been delivering the same admonitions for two years, they sit silent and contrite, like schoolkids whose homework the dog ate. This isn’t just a Modi-era phenomenon. At the 2007 CII AGM, then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh had chided corporate leaders for paying themselves too much. The irony: The mood and message then were opposite to now. Sunil Mittal, then CII chief, responded by pledging ‘a significant part of his salary bonus’ to charity. I had then written, and repeated in a 2013 column, that corporate India has to grow the spine to tell the Prime Minister he didn’t fix their wages. He should leave them alone if they paid their taxes honestly. Of course, no such thing happened. Corporate India also swallowed that retrograde idea of near-mandatory corporate social responsibility. Even at Ficci, and in the corporate and financial universe, too many good people have too many important points to make. But nobody would dare. Corporate India is waiting for its next Rahul Bajaj. Or preferably a few of them.
